question: What is DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC?
title: DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC — Front Controller Pattern
direct_answer: DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller — a single servlet that intercepts every incoming HTTP request and routes it to the correct handler (controller method). It implements the Front Controller design pattern. Spring Boot auto-configures it at URL pattern `/`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring MVC request processing pipeline and the role of the front controller pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking controllers directly handle HTTP requests — DispatcherServlet is the single entry point that orchestrates the entire request flow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the full request lifecycle: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Controller → ViewResolver/MessageConverter → Response, mentioning each component's responsibility

sections.title: The Front Controller of Spring MVC
sections.content:
**DispatcherServlet** is the central entry point for all HTTP requests in a Spring MVC application.

Think of it as a receptionist at a large office building — instead of visitors going directly to individual offices (controllers), they check in at the front desk first. The receptionist (DispatcherServlet) looks up which office to send them to, guides them there, collects the response, and delivers it back. This is the **Front Controller pattern** — one component handles all requests and delegates to specialized handlers. Without DispatcherServlet, you'd need separate servlets for every endpoint. Spring Boot automatically registers it at the root URL pattern `/` when you include spring-boot-starter-web, so every request — `/api/users`, `/health`, even `/favicon.ico` — passes through DispatcherServlet first. It doesn't do the actual business logic; it **orchestrates** the request flow by coordinating with HandlerMapping, Controller, ViewResolver, and MessageConverter components.

sections.title: Request Flow Through DispatcherServlet
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[HTTP Request] --> B[DispatcherServlet
front controller] B --> C[HandlerMapping
find controller method] C --> D[HandlerAdapter
invoke method] D --> E[Controller method runs] E --> F[HttpMessageConverter
object to JSON] F --> G[HTTP Response] ```

sections.title: DispatcherServlet in Action with Spring Boot
When DispatcherServlet Comes Into Play
sections.content:
You rely on DispatcherServlet whenever you build a **Spring MVC REST API or web application**. If you're using Spring Boot with spring-boot-starter-web, it's already there — you don't configure it manually.

Use DispatcherServlet when you need **centralized request handling** with Spring's ecosystem: dependency injection in controllers, declarative validation with @Valid, AOP-based transaction management, or HandlerInterceptors for cross-cutting concerns. If you're building a pure servlet-based app without Spring, you'd write individual servlets per endpoint. But in Spring MVC, DispatcherServlet handles routing for all endpoints through a single entry point.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking controllers are servlets**: Freshers often believe each @RestController is a servlet that directly receives HTTP requests. In reality, controllers are plain Spring beans — DispatcherServlet is the only servlet, and it delegates to controllers.
- **Not understanding why URL patterns matter**: If you manually register DispatcherServlet with pattern `/api/*`, requests to `/health` won't reach it. Spring Boot registers it at `/` so all requests go through it.
- **Assuming DispatcherServlet does business logic**: It's purely a coordinator — it routes requests, invokes handlers, and formats responses, but never contains your domain logic.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Front Controller Pattern**: DispatcherServlet is the single entry point that intercepts all HTTP requests and delegates to appropriate handlers
**Auto-Configuration**: Spring Boot registers DispatcherServlet at URL pattern `/` when spring-boot-starter-web is on classpath — no manual configuration needed
**Request Flow**: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping (finds controller method) → HandlerAdapter (invokes method) → ViewResolver/MessageConverter (formats response)
**Controllers Are Not Servlets**: @RestController classes are Spring beans — DispatcherServlet is the only servlet that calls their methods
**HttpServletRequest/Response**: DispatcherServlet wraps these low-level objects and exposes cleaner abstractions like @PathVariable and ResponseEntity to controllers
**Exception Handling**: When a controller throws an exception, DispatcherServlet consults @ControllerAdvice classes to convert it into an HTTP error response
**Context Hierarchy**: DispatcherServlet has its own WebApplicationContext (child) that holds controllers, while the root context holds services and repositories

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: DispatcherServlet is the front controller in Spring MVC — it's the single servlet that handles every HTTP request coming into your application. Think of it as a traffic cop directing requests to the right place. When a request hits your Spring Boot app, DispatcherServlet intercepts it first. It doesn't process the request itself — instead, it uses HandlerMapping to figure out which controller method should handle it, then invokes that method through a HandlerAdapter. After the controller returns a result, DispatcherServlet uses MessageConverters like Jackson to turn your Java object into JSON for the response. Spring Boot automatically configures DispatcherServlet for you at the root URL pattern slash when you add spring-boot-starter-web. One common mistake freshers make is thinking each controller is a separate servlet. That's not true — DispatcherServlet is the only servlet, and controllers are just Spring beans it calls. Another pitfall is not realizing that HandlerInterceptors and exception handlers only work because DispatcherServlet orchestrates them. Without DispatcherServlet, you'd need separate servlets for every endpoint, which would be painful. In production REST APIs, DispatcherServlet handles thousands of requests per second, routing each to the correct controller method based on URL path, HTTP method, headers, and content type. It's the backbone of Spring MVC.

question: What is ViewResolver in Spring MVC?
title: ViewResolver in Spring MVC — Resolving View Names to Templates
direct_answer: ViewResolver resolves a view name string returned by a @Controller method into an actual view template. For example, InternalResourceViewResolver maps "users" to /WEB-INF/views/users.jsp. ThymeleafViewResolver maps it to templates/users.html.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how traditional @Controller view resolution works for server-side HTML rendering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ViewResolver is used in REST APIs — it's only for @Controller methods returning view names, not @RestController returning JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ContentNegotiatingViewResolver for multiple view types, and explain that @RestController bypasses ViewResolver entirely because @ResponseBody is implicit

sections.title: How ViewResolver Connects Controller Methods to HTML Templates
sections.content:
When you build a traditional server-side rendered web app with Spring MVC, your **@Controller** methods return logical view names like "userList" instead of actual HTML. The **ViewResolver** takes that string and resolves it to a physical template file. WHY does Spring do this? Decoupling. Your controller doesn't care if you're using JSP, Thymeleaf, or Freemarker — you just return a view name.

HOW it works: Spring holds a chain of ViewResolver beans. When DispatcherServlet gets a view name from your controller, it asks each resolver in order to find a matching view. The first one that can resolve it wins. Think of ViewResolver like a phone book — you give it a name, it looks up the full address. **InternalResourceViewResolver** is the classic JSP resolver, **ThymeleafViewResolver** handles Thymeleaf templates. In modern REST APIs with **@RestController**, ViewResolver is never invoked because @ResponseBody tells Spring to write the object directly to the HTTP response body, not render a view.

sections.title: ViewResolver at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@Controller path|~Returns a view name|"users" is logical|ViewResolver finds the file|server-side HTML
blue|InternalResourceViewResolver|~JSP rendering|prefix + suffix|/WEB-INF/views/users.jsp|classic stack
emerald|ThymeleafViewResolver|~Spring Boot default|looks in templates/|templates/users.html|modern engine
rose|@RestController bypass|~No view resolution|@ResponseBody implicit|object to JSON directly|ViewResolver never runs

sections.title: Traditional MVC Controller with ViewResolver
When ViewResolver Matters in Real Projects
sections.content: Use ViewResolver when you're building **server-side rendered web applications** where the backend generates HTML pages. Typical scenarios: (1) Admin dashboards or internal tools where SEO and JavaScript frameworks aren't priorities — Spring MVC with Thymeleaf is faster to develop than a separate React frontend. (2) Multi-page applications (MPAs) where each route renders a full page refresh, common in enterprise intranets. (3) Form-heavy workflows like checkout flows or wizards where you want server-side validation and rendering. Do NOT use ViewResolver in REST APIs. If your controller methods return JSON to a React or Angular frontend, you need @RestController, not @Controller with views.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Controller instead of @RestController for REST APIs**: Freshers add ViewResolver config to a REST API project, then wonder why they get 404 errors. If you're returning JSON, use @RestController which has implicit @ResponseBody on every method — ViewResolver is never called.
- **Forgetting template files in the classpath**: You configure ThymeleafViewResolver but put templates in src/main/webapp instead of src/main/resources/templates. Spring Boot's default resolver looks in classpath:templates/, not webapp.
- **Returning view names from @RestController methods**: If you accidentally use @RestController and return a String, Spring treats it as the response body (literal string), not a view name. You'll see "userList" as plain text in the browser instead of rendered HTML.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **ViewResolver**: maps logical view names from @Controller methods to physical template files like JSP or Thymeleaf
**InternalResourceViewResolver**: classic resolver for JSP files, uses prefix and suffix properties to build full path
**ThymeleafViewResolver**: Spring Boot auto-configures this when spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf is on classpath
**@RestController bypass**: @RestController has implicit @ResponseBody, so DispatcherServlet writes objects directly to response without invoking ViewResolver
**ContentNegotiatingViewResolver**: advanced resolver that selects view type based on Accept header, useful for supporting both HTML and JSON from same controller
**Model attribute**: data passed from controller to view via Model.addAttribute, accessible in template as expression variables
**View resolution chain**: Spring tries each registered ViewResolver in order until one returns a non-null View object

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ViewResolver is the component that connects a controller method's return value to an actual HTML template. When you use at-Controller and return a string like users, that's a logical view name. Spring doesn't know where the template file lives yet. The ViewResolver takes that name and resolves it to the physical file. For example, InternalResourceViewResolver is configured with a prefix like slash-WEB-INF-slash-views-slash and a suffix like dot-jsp. So it turns users into slash-WEB-INF-slash-views-slash-users-dot-jsp. Thymeleaf works the same way but looks in the templates folder by default. Here's the key thing freshers miss — ViewResolver is only used in traditional server-side rendered apps with at-Controller. If you're building a REST API with at-RestController, ViewResolver never gets invoked because at-ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize your object to JSON directly. The response body isn't a view, it's the data itself. One advanced detail — ContentNegotiatingViewResolver can pick different view types based on the Accept header, so the same controller method can return HTML or JSON depending on what the client requests. That's rare in practice though. Most projects either use at-Controller for web pages or at-RestController for APIs, not both in the same endpoint.

question: What is HandlerMapping in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerMapping in Spring MVC — URL to Controller Method Resolution
direct_answer: HandlerMapping is the Spring MVC component that determines which controller method should handle an incoming HTTP request based on URL path, HTTP method, headers, and parameters. RequestMappingHandlerMapping is the default implementation — it scans @RequestMapping annotations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of Spring MVC internal knowledge beyond just writing @GetMapping annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing HandlerMapping exists — thinking Spring magically routes requests without understanding the lookup mechanism
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multiple HandlerMapping beans can exist with different priorities, and Spring tries them in order until one returns a handler

sections.title: The Request Router in Spring MVC
sections.content:
**HandlerMapping** is the component responsible for finding which controller method (handler) should process an incoming HTTP request. Imagine you send a GET request to `/api/users/42`.

DispatcherServlet receives it and asks HandlerMapping: "Which method handles this?" HandlerMapping scans all registered controller methods, checks their **@RequestMapping** annotations (or shortcuts like @GetMapping), and returns the matching method. The most common implementation is **RequestMappingHandlerMapping**, which Spring Boot configures automatically. It builds an internal map during startup: URL pattern + HTTP method → controller method. When a request arrives, it performs a fast lookup in this map. HandlerMapping doesn't invoke the method — it just returns a **HandlerExecutionChain** (the matched method plus any interceptors) back to DispatcherServlet. This separation of concerns keeps routing logic isolated from execution logic. Multiple HandlerMapping beans can coexist with different **order priorities**, so Spring tries them sequentially until one returns a handler.

sections.title: HandlerMapping at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|RequestMappingHandlerMapping|~Default implementation|scans @RequestMapping|builds URL to method map|runs at startup
blue|Runtime lookup|~Per request|matches path + HTTP method|returns HandlerExecutionChain|includes interceptors
emerald|Multiple mappings|~Ordered by priority|controllers + static resources|tried in sequence|first match wins
rose|Ambiguous mapping|~Two identical patterns|fails fast at startup|AmbiguousMappingException|fix duplicate routes

sections.title: How HandlerMapping Resolves Controller Methods
When HandlerMapping Matters
sections.content: You interact with HandlerMapping indirectly every time you write **@GetMapping, @PostMapping, or @RequestMapping** — those annotations tell RequestMappingHandlerMapping how to route requests. You'd explicitly configure custom HandlerMapping beans when building **non-standard routing logic**: routing based on custom headers, versioning APIs through Accept headers (Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json), or serving static resources through ResourceHandlerMapping. In most Spring Boot REST APIs, the default RequestMappingHandlerMapping handles everything. But understanding it helps debug routing conflicts — like two methods with overlapping patterns — because HandlerMapping throws AmbiguousMappingException when it can't decide.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing HandlerMapping exists**: Freshers think Spring "just knows" which method to call. They don't realize DispatcherServlet delegates to HandlerMapping for this lookup. When routing breaks, they don't know where to look.
- **Assuming only one HandlerMapping**: Spring registers several by default — RequestMappingHandlerMapping for controllers, SimpleUrlHandlerMapping for static resources. If you register a custom one without setting order, it might not run.
- **Conflicting mappings without realizing**: Writing two methods with @GetMapping("/users/{id}") and @GetMapping("/users/{name}") causes AmbiguousMappingException at startup because HandlerMapping can't distinguish them — freshers think "oh, one's an id, one's a name" but HandlerMapping sees identical patterns.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Routing Responsibility**: HandlerMapping's only job is finding which controller method matches an incoming request — it doesn't invoke the method or process the response
**RequestMappingHandlerMapping**: The default implementation that scans @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping annotations and builds an internal routing map at startup
**Multiple HandlerMappings**: Spring can have several HandlerMapping beans with different order values — DispatcherServlet tries them sequentially until one returns a match
**HandlerExecutionChain**: HandlerMapping returns this object containing the matched handler method plus any HandlerInterceptors that apply to it
**Pattern Matching**: Supports path variables like /users/{id}, wildcards like /docs/**, and HTTP method filtering — all configured through annotation attributes
**Ambiguous Mappings**: If two methods have identical patterns, HandlerMapping throws AmbiguousMappingException at startup — it can't decide which to use
**Static Resources**: ResourceHandlerMapping (another implementation) routes requests to static files in src/main/resources/static without hitting controllers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HandlerMapping is the component that figures out which controller method should handle an HTTP request. When DispatcherServlet receives a request, it doesn't know which controller to call — that's HandlerMapping's job. The default implementation is RequestMappingHandlerMapping. During application startup, it scans all your controllers, finds every method with annotations like at-GetMapping or at-PostMapping, and builds an internal map: URL pattern plus HTTP method to controller method. For example, if you have at-GetMapping slash users slash id, it creates a mapping from GET slash users slash curly-brace-id to that method. At runtime, when a request comes in for GET slash users slash 42, HandlerMapping looks it up in the map and returns the matching method wrapped in a HandlerExecutionChain, which also includes any interceptors. One thing freshers often miss is that multiple HandlerMapping beans can exist. Spring Boot registers RequestMappingHandlerMapping for your controllers and SimpleUrlHandlerMapping for static resources. They have order priorities, so DispatcherServlet tries them in sequence until one returns a match. A common mistake is creating ambiguous mappings — like two methods with at-GetMapping slash users slash id. HandlerMapping can't tell them apart and throws AmbiguousMappingException at startup. Understanding HandlerMapping helps you debug routing issues and customize routing behavior beyond simple annotations.

question: What happens when a Spring Boot application starts with Spring MVC?
title: Spring MVC Auto-Configuration at Startup — What Spring Boot Does
direct_answer: On startup, Spring Boot auto-configures: registers DispatcherServlet at `/`, creates RequestMappingHandlerMapping by scanning all @Controller beans, configures Jackson as the default JSON HttpMessageConverter, sets up ViewResolvers for Thymeleaf if present, and registers default exception handlers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot auto-configuration for Spring MVC and what happens behind the scenes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing why adding spring-boot-starter-web is sufficient to get a working REST API — magic is auto-configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WebMvcAutoConfiguration class and how adding @EnableWebMvc disables auto-configuration, forcing manual configuration

sections.title: Spring Boot's Auto-Configuration for MVC
sections.content:
When a Spring Boot application starts with **spring-boot-starter-web** on the classpath, Spring Boot's auto-configuration kicks in and sets up a fully functional web application without you writing any XML or configuration classes. The **WebMvcAutoConfiguration** class (in spring-boot-autoconfigure) detects that you want a web app and performs dozens of registration steps: it creates and registers **DispatcherServlet** at the root URL pattern `/`, scans all **@Controller** and **@RestController** beans to build **RequestMappingHandlerMapping**, registers **Jackson's ObjectMapper** as the default **HttpMessageConverter** for JSON serialization, sets up **content negotiation** (Accept headers), configures **static resource handling** for `/static`, `/public`, `/resources` folders, and registers **default error handling** through BasicErrorController (the `/error` endpoint). If you have Thymeleaf on the classpath, it auto-configures ThymeleafViewResolver. This is why you can write a single @RestController class and immediately have a working REST API — the infrastructure is wired automatically.

The key insight: **convention over configuration**. Spring Boot assumes sensible defaults so freshers can build production-ready apps without deep Spring MVC knowledge.

sections.title: Spring Boot MVC Startup Sequence
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[main starts
SpringApplication.run] --> B[Application context boots] B --> C[WebMvcAutoConfiguration] C --> D[Register DispatcherServlet at /] D --> E[Scan @Controller beans
build HandlerMapping] E --> F[Register Jackson converter] F --> G[Embedded Tomcat on 8080
ready for requests] ```

sections.title: Minimal Spring Boot REST API with Auto-Configuration
When Auto-Configuration Applies
sections.content:
Spring Boot's MVC auto-configuration applies whenever you include **spring-boot-starter-web** in your dependencies and don't use **@EnableWebMvc** annotation. This covers most modern Spring Boot REST APIs and web apps.

Use it when you want **rapid development** without boilerplate configuration — building microservices, internal APIs, admin dashboards, or prototypes. Auto-configuration handles the 90% use case: JSON REST APIs with Jackson, embedded servlet containers, static resource serving, and basic error handling. If you need **custom MVC configuration** like adding interceptors, custom message converters, or CORS settings, you can still keep auto-configuration — just implement **WebMvcConfigurer** interface in a @Configuration class. Only disable auto-configuration (by adding @EnableWebMvc) when you need **full manual control**, which is rare in modern Spring Boot apps.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not understanding why it works**: Freshers add spring-boot-starter-web and write a controller — it works, but they don't know DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, and Jackson were auto-configured. This bites them when troubleshooting.
- **Adding @EnableWebMvc accidentally**: This annotation disables Spring Boot's auto-configuration, forcing you to manually configure everything. Freshers copy it from old Spring tutorials and wonder why their app breaks.
- **Assuming manual beans override auto-config**: If you define your own ObjectMapper bean, Spring Boot's auto-configured one backs off. Freshers don't realize this and create duplicate beans without understanding the conditional logic.
- **Not checking auto-configuration report**: Running with --debug flag shows which auto-configurations applied — freshers never look at this when debugging configuration issues.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **WebMvcAutoConfiguration**: The Spring Boot class that auto-configures DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, MessageConverters, ViewResolvers, and static resource handling
**DispatcherServlet Registration**: Automatically registered at URL pattern / with load-on-startup so it's ready before first request arrives
**Jackson Integration**: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter auto-configured when Jackson is on classpath — handles JSON serialization for @RestController methods
**RequestMappingHandlerMapping**: Scans all @Controller and @RestController beans during startup and builds routing map from annotations
**Static Resources**: Serves files from /static, /public, /resources, /META-INF/resources in classpath without requiring controller methods
**@EnableWebMvc Disables Auto-Config**: Using this annotation tells Spring Boot you want full manual control — auto-configuration backs off completely
**Conditional Beans**: Auto-configuration uses @ConditionalOnMissingBean — if you define your own DispatcherServlet or ObjectMapper, auto-config skips those

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a Spring Boot application starts with spring-boot-starter-web, auto-configuration wires up the entire Spring MVC infrastructure automatically. The key player is WebMvcAutoConfiguration — a configuration class in Spring Boot that runs at startup. It registers DispatcherServlet at the root URL pattern slash, so every HTTP request goes through it. Then it scans all your at-Controller and at-RestController beans to create RequestMappingHandlerMapping, which builds the routing map from annotations like at-GetMapping. Spring Boot also detects Jackson on the classpath and registers it as the default HttpMessageConverter, so your controller methods can return Java objects and they'll be automatically serialized to JSON. If you have Thymeleaf or another template engine, Spring Boot configures the appropriate ViewResolver. It also sets up static resource handling for folders like slash static and slash public, and registers a default error handler at slash error for unhandled exceptions. The beauty is you don't write any of this — just adding the starter dependency and writing a controller is enough. A critical point freshers miss: if you add at-EnableWebMvc annotation, you disable all this auto-configuration. That annotation is from old Spring MVC — it tells Spring Boot you want manual control. Suddenly your app breaks because DispatcherServlet isn't registered, Jackson isn't configured, nothing works. Spring Boot's philosophy is convention over configuration — sensible defaults let you build production-ready apps fast, and you only customize what's different.

question: What is a HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC — Pre and Post Processing
direct_answer: HandlerInterceptor intercepts HTTP requests at the Spring MVC layer — before and after controller method execution. Used for cross-cutting concerns: authentication checks, logging, timing, rate limiting. It's Spring MVC's equivalent of a filter but operates within the Spring context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring MVC's interceptor mechanism for cross-cutting concerns and how it differs from servlet filters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring HandlerInterceptor with Servlet Filter — both intercept requests but at different layers with different capabilities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three methods: preHandle runs before controller, postHandle runs after controller but before response, afterCompletion runs after response is sent

sections.title: Request Interceptors in Spring MVC
sections.content:
**HandlerInterceptor** is Spring MVC's mechanism for intercepting HTTP requests at three points in the request lifecycle: before the controller method executes, after it returns but before the response is written, and after the response is fully sent.

Think of it as **middleware** that wraps around your controller logic. Unlike **Servlet Filters**, which operate at the servlet container level and see raw HttpServletRequest objects, HandlerInterceptors run **inside Spring's context** after DispatcherServlet has resolved the handler but before it invokes the controller method. This gives you access to Spring beans, @Autowired dependencies, and the actual controller method that will handle the request. Common use cases: **authentication** (check JWT token before controller runs), **logging** (record request details and execution time), **rate limiting** (block excessive requests from same IP), **tenant resolution** (in multi-tenant apps, extract tenant ID from header and set it in ThreadLocal). HandlerInterceptors are registered globally or for specific URL patterns through **WebMvcConfigurer**, and multiple interceptors form an execution chain.

sections.title: HandlerInterceptor Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Request] --> B[preHandle] B -->|returns true| C[Controller method] B -->|returns false| X[Request aborted] C --> D[postHandle] D --> E[Response written] E --> F[afterCompletion
always runs, even on exception] ```

sections.title: Implementing a Logging HandlerInterceptor
When to Use HandlerInterceptor vs Servlet Filter
sections.content:
Use **HandlerInterceptor** when you need **Spring-specific features**: access to the matched controller method (handler object), dependency injection of Spring beans, or modification of ModelAndView in traditional MVC apps. Best for **authentication/authorization** (you know which method is about to run, can check method-level @Secured annotations), **request logging** with controller context, **tenant or locale resolution** (need to set data in Spring's context for controllers to use).

Use **Servlet Filter** for **lower-level concerns** that must apply even to static resources or non-Spring endpoints: CORS headers (need to set headers before Spring MVC runs), compression, encoding, or security filters that inspect raw request bytes. Filters see every request; HandlerInterceptors only run for requests that match a controller. In practice, most Spring Boot apps use HandlerInterceptors for business concerns and rely on Spring Security's filters for authentication, because Security integrates with the filter chain directly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing with Servlet Filters**: Freshers hear "intercepts requests" and think it's the same as Filter. But HandlerInterceptor runs after DispatcherServlet resolves the handler — so it has access to the controller method and Spring context. Filters run before DispatcherServlet even sees the request.
- **Returning false in preHandle without setting response**: If preHandle returns false, Spring short-circuits — the controller doesn't run. Freshers forget to write an error response, so the client gets an empty 200 OK.
- **Assuming postHandle runs on exception**: If the controller throws an exception, postHandle is skipped. Only afterCompletion runs, and it receives the exception as a parameter.
- **Not registering the interceptor**: Writing a HandlerInterceptor class but forgetting to add it to InterceptorRegistry means it never runs — freshers wonder why their logging doesn't work.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Three Lifecycle Methods**: preHandle runs before controller; postHandle runs after controller but before response; afterCompletion runs after response is sent, even if exception occurred
**Spring Context Access**: HandlerInterceptor runs inside Spring MVC — you can @Autowire services, access the handler method object, and modify ModelAndView
**Short-Circuit with preHandle**: Returning false from preHandle stops the request — controller doesn't run, postHandle doesn't run, only afterCompletion runs
**Execution Chain**: Multiple HandlerInterceptors execute in order — preHandle in forward order, postHandle and afterCompletion in reverse order
**URL Pattern Filtering**: Register interceptors for specific paths like /api/** or exclude paths with excludePathPatterns — more flexible than Filter's servlet mapping
**Exception Handling**: postHandle is skipped if controller throws exception, but afterCompletion still runs with the exception passed as a parameter
**vs Servlet Filter**: Filters run before DispatcherServlet sees the request; HandlerInterceptors run after DispatcherServlet resolves the handler but before it invokes the controller

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HandlerInterceptor is Spring MVC's way to intercept requests before and after they hit your controller methods. It's useful for cross-cutting concerns like authentication, logging, or timing. When a request comes in, DispatcherServlet uses HandlerMapping to find the matching controller method, then before calling that method, it runs all registered HandlerInterceptors. The interceptor interface has three methods. preHandle runs before the controller — you can check authentication here and return false to block the request. If you return true, Spring continues to the controller. After the controller finishes, postHandle runs — you can modify the ModelAndView here, but in REST APIs we usually don't need this. Finally, afterCompletion runs after the response is fully sent, even if the controller threw an exception. This is where you'd log timing or clean up resources. A key difference from Servlet Filters: HandlerInterceptors run inside Spring's context, so you can at-Autowire beans and access the actual handler method object. Filters run at the servlet container level, before DispatcherServlet even processes the request. Freshers often confuse the two because both intercept requests. One common mistake is returning false from preHandle without writing an error response — the client gets an empty reply. Another is assuming postHandle runs when an exception occurs — it doesn't, only afterCompletion runs in that case. HandlerInterceptors are perfect for request logging, rate limiting, or tenant resolution in multi-tenant apps.

speakable_v2.hook: HandlerInterceptor and Servlet Filter both intercept requests — but they live at different layers and see different things.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: A Servlet Filter runs at the servlet container level, before DispatcherServlet even sees the request. It has no access to the Spring context and doesn't know which controller will handle the request.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: A HandlerInterceptor runs inside the Spring MVC layer, after DispatcherServlet has identified the handler. It has full access to the Spring context and knows which controller method is about to be called.

beats.label: differences
content: preHandle: runs before the controller method. Return false to abort the request entirely.
postHandle: runs after the controller method but before the response is written. Can modify ModelAndView.
afterCompletion: runs after the complete response, even if an exception was thrown. Good for cleanup and timing.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use a Filter for concerns that apply regardless of Spring — encoding, security at the container level. Use HandlerInterceptor when you need Spring beans injected or need to know which controller is running — logging, role-based access checks against your user service.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: non-obvious: postHandle is only called if the controller method succeeded. If the method throws an exception, postHandle is skipped. afterCompletion is always called — that's the right place for guaranteed cleanup.

question: What is HttpMessageConverter in Spring MVC?
title: HttpMessageConverter in Spring — Serialization and Deserialization
direct_answer: HttpMessageConverter converts Java objects to HTTP response bodies (serialization) and HTTP request bodies to Java objects (deserialization). MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter handles JSON. Spring Boot auto-configures it when Jackson is on the classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how @RequestBody and @ResponseBody actually work under the hood
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Jackson just works magically without understanding the MessageConverter chain and content negotiation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain content negotiation — Spring selects the converter based on Accept and Content-Type headers, trying each registered converter in order

sections.title: How Spring Converts Between Java Objects and HTTP Bodies
sections.content:
When your **@RestController** method returns a Java object, Spring needs to convert it to JSON (or XML, or another format) for the HTTP response body. Conversely, when a client POSTs JSON to a **@RequestBody** parameter, Spring needs to deserialize that JSON into your Java object. That's what **HttpMessageConverter** does — bidirectional conversion between Java objects and HTTP message bodies. WHY is this needed? HTTP only transmits bytes. Your application works with POJOs. There's a fundamental impedance mismatch.

HOW it works: Spring maintains a list of registered HttpMessageConverter implementations. When processing a response, Spring iterates through them asking "can you write this object for the requested media type?" The first converter that returns true does the job. **MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter** handles JSON using the Jackson library. **Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter** handles XML. Spring Boot automatically registers converters when it detects libraries on the classpath — if Jackson is present, you get JSON support out of the box.

Think of it like a translation service at an airport — you speak Java, the client speaks JSON, the converter translates both ways.

sections.title: HttpMessageConverter at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Serialization|~Java object to body|@ResponseBody return|MappingJackson2 writes JSON|outgoing response
blue|Deserialization|~Body to Java object|@RequestBody parameter|Jackson reads JSON|incoming request
emerald|Content negotiation|~Picks the converter|Accept header for write|Content-Type for read|first match wins
rose|No matching converter|~Media type unsupported|returns 406|add jackson-dataformat-xml for XML|JSON works by default

sections.title: Using HttpMessageConverter with @RequestBody and @ResponseBody
When HttpMessageConverter Is Active in Your API
sections.content: HttpMessageConverter is used automatically in every **@RestController** method with @RequestBody or @ResponseBody (which is implicit in @RestController). Concrete scenarios: (1) Building a REST API where Angular or React frontend sends JSON to your backend — the converter deserializes the request body into your DTO. (2) Microservice communication using RestTemplate or WebClient — when you call restTemplate.postForObject(), the converter serializes your request object to JSON. (3) Content negotiation scenarios where the same endpoint can return JSON or XML depending on the Accept header — Spring selects the appropriate converter. (4) Custom serialization needs like excluding null fields or formatting dates — you configure the ObjectMapper bean that MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses. You don't manually invoke converters in your code. Spring's DispatcherServlet and RequestMappingHandlerAdapter handle it transparently based on annotations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting Jackson dependency in non-Boot projects**: Freshers expect JSON to work without adding Jackson to pom.xml. Spring Boot includes it by default, but plain Spring MVC doesn't. Without a JSON converter, you get 406 Not Acceptable errors.
- **Not understanding Content-Type vs Accept headers**: They send JSON but forget Content-Type: application/json header, so Spring can't find a converter to read the request body. Or they expect JSON response but the Accept header says text/html, so Spring picks StringHttpMessageConverter instead.
- **Returning raw List from @RestController**: Returning List<User> works because MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter handles collections, but freshers think they need to manually convert it to JSON string first. Never call ObjectMapper yourself in a controller — the converter does it.
- **Assuming XML support exists by default**: Jackson handles JSON automatically in Boot, but XML requires adding jackson-dataformat-xml dependency. Without it, clients requesting application/xml get 406 errors.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **HttpMessageConverter**: interface for bidirectional conversion between HTTP message bodies and Java objects
**MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter**: default JSON converter, auto-configured when Jackson library is on classpath
**@RequestBody**: triggers message converter to deserialize HTTP request body into method parameter object
**@ResponseBody**: triggers message converter to serialize method return value into HTTP response body
**Content negotiation**: Spring selects converter based on Content-Type header (request) and Accept header (response)
**Converter chain**: Spring tries each registered HttpMessageConverter in order, first one supporting the media type wins
**ObjectMapper customization**: customize JSON serialization by defining an ObjectMapper bean, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses it automatically

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: HttpMessageConverter is the mechanism that Spring uses to convert between Java objects and HTTP request or response bodies. When you put at-RequestBody on a parameter, Spring needs to read the JSON from the request and turn it into your Java object. That's deserialization. When your at-RestController method returns an object, Spring needs to write that object as JSON to the response. That's serialization. Both are done by HttpMessageConverter. The most important one is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter which handles JSON using the Jackson library. Spring Boot automatically configures it when Jackson is on the classpath, which is why JSON just works out of the box. Here's how content negotiation fits in. Spring maintains a list of registered converters. When a request comes in, it looks at the Content-Type header to pick a converter for reading the body. When preparing the response, it looks at the Accept header to pick a converter for writing. It tries each converter in order until one says I can handle this media type. If none match, you get a 406 Not Acceptable error. One thing freshers miss — you never manually call these converters in your controller code. Spring's DispatcherServlet does it automatically based on annotations. If you find yourself calling ObjectMapper dot writeValueAsString in a controller, you're doing it wrong. Let the framework handle it through at-ResponseBody or at-RestController.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: When you return a Java object from a @RestController, something has to turn it into JSON bytes. That something is HttpMessageConverter.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: HttpMessageConverter handles both directions: it reads incoming request bodies and writes outgoing response bodies. For JSON, the default converter is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, auto-configured when Jackson is on the classpath.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Spring selects the right converter using content negotiation. For writing a response, it checks the Accept header the client sent. For reading a request body, it checks the Content-Type header. If you send JSON with Content-Type application/json, Spring uses Jackson to deserialize it into your @RequestBody parameter.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter: handles JSON. Auto-configured. Used for most REST APIs.
StringHttpMessageConverter: for String return types, produces text/plain.
ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter: for binary data like file downloads.
Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter: handles XML if jackson-dataformat-xml is on the classpath.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: If a client sends Accept: application/xml but you only have the JSON converter configured, Spring returns 406 Not Acceptable — not a serialization error. The converter chain is checked before your method return value is touched.

speakable_v2.cap: Customize Jackson by defining an ObjectMapper bean — Spring Boot will use yours instead of the default configuration.
